items.title: Negation & questions
items.subtitle: Saying no and asking questions with elegance
objectifs: Negate a noun (değil) and a verb (-me)

blocks.text: Negating « to be »: değil

To negate « I am… », Turkish uses the word değil (not to be), placed after the noun, and it takes the personal endings itself: Öğretmen değilim (I am not a teacher), Hasta değilsin (you are not ill), Türk değil (he is not Turkish).
Negating a verb: -me/-ma

For verbs, negation is a -me/-ma block glued to the root, before the tense: gelmiyorum (I am not coming), yapmadım (I did not do it), gitmeyeceğim (I will not go). One -me is enough to negate the whole verb.
The question: mi, mı, mu, mü

The question particle goes after the word being asked about and is written separately (with a hyphen in textbooks: mı-). It harmonises with the last vowel of the preceding word, like a detached suffix.

items.fr: Are you a student?
Are you coming?
Is this (really) a pencil?
Did you understand?
Are you Turkish?
Is there any coffee?

blocks.text: mi questions the word immediately before it: Yarın mı geliyorsun? (= is it tomorrow that you are coming?) ≠ Yarın geliyor musun? (= are you coming tomorrow?). Turkish does not need inversion: you simply « mark » what you are in doubt about.
In casual speech, a simple rising intonation is enough too: <tur>Geliyorsun?</tur> (you are coming?). But the form with mi remains the reference in writing.

dialogue.title: So, are you coming or not?

lines.name: Elif
lines.fr: Are you coming to the party tomorrow?

lines.name: Magloire
lines.fr: I am not coming, unfortunately. I am very tired.

lines.name: Elif
lines.fr: Why aren't you coming? Don't you like parties?

lines.name: Magloire
lines.tr: Hayır, partileri seviyorum. Ama sınavım var.
lines.fr: No, I do like parties. But I have an exam.

lines.name: Elif
lines.tr: Ha, anladım! Sınav mı? Ne zaman?
lines.fr: Ah, I see! An exam? When?

lines.name: Magloire
lines.fr: On Saturday. I'll be studying at the weekend.

lines.name: Elif
lines.fr: All right, good luck in advance!

quiz.exp: değil + -im = I am not.
The preceding word (geliyor) ends in o/u (back, rounded) → mı. Geliyor musun?
Türk ends in ü → mü: Türk müsünüz?

quiz.q: Where does the question particle go?
opts: always at the start of the sentence
after the word being asked about
at the end of the sentence only
quiz.exp: It follows the word in doubt: its position defines what you are asking about.

items.title: At the restaurant: the first cases
items.subtitle: Locative, accusative, dative: ordering like a local
objectifs: Understand the accusative of a definite object
Order food and ask for the bill

blocks.text: Turkish replaces French prepositions (to, in, on, towards…) with case suffixes glued to the end of the noun. There are six; this module teaches you the three most useful ones at the restaurant.
The locative: -de / -da (in, at, on)

If the word ends in a voiceless consonant (p, ç, t, k, s, ş, f, h), the d of the suffix becomes t: sokak → sokakta, et → ette, iş → işte. A handy mnemonic for the voiceless ones: « p ç t k s ş f h »: fresh Turkish fish cooks quickly.
The accusative: the definite object (-i, -ı, -u, -ü)
A key subtlety: the accusative does not mark just any object, but the definite object — the one already known. Compare:

items.fr: I bought bread. (indefinite: bread in general)
I took the bread. (definite: the one we were expecting)
I am reading (books). (general activity)
I am reading the book. (that particular book)

blocks.text: After a final vowel, a buffer y slips in: masa-y-ı (the table), kapı-y-ı (the door), çay-ı (the tea).
The dative: -e / -a (to, towards)

It marks the destination: <tur>Eve gidiyorum</tur> (I am going home), <tur>Okula gittik</tur> (we went to school), <tur>Masaya koydum</tur> (I put it on the table). After a vowel, add buffer y: <tur>araba-y-a</tur>.
Restaurant survival kit

items.fr: Could I have a menu?

items.tr: İki kebap ve bir ayran, lütfen.
items.fr: Two kebabs and one ayran, please.
Could we have the bill?
It was delicious!
Shall we leave a tip?

blocks.text: alabilir miyim? (may I…) turns any request into a polite formula: Su alabilir miyim?, Oturabilir miyim?. Add efendim for a very courteous tone.

lines.name: Magloire
lines.fr: Thank you. Could I have the menu?

lines.name: Garson
lines.fr: Of course, here you go. What would you like to drink?

lines.name: Magloire
lines.tr: Ben bir ayran, Elif bir şalgam istiyor.

lines.name: Elif
lines.tr: Yok yok, ben de ayran içiyorum!
lines.fr: No, no, I'm having an ayran too!

lines.name: Garson
lines.fr: What would you like to eat?

lines.name: Magloire
lines.tr: İki Adana kebabı, lütfen. Acısız olsun.
lines.fr: Two Adana kebabs, please. Not spicy.

lines.name: Garson

quiz.exp: -de = locative: in/at home.
After a voiceless consonant (k), d → t: sokaKTA. Likewise: işte, otobüste.

opts: I am going to the bread
quiz.exp: The accusative -i marks the definite object: the bread in question.

alabilir miyim = « may I have… », the all-purpose polite formula.

items.title: The past: -di and -miş
items.subtitle: Telling what you saw… and what you heard

blocks.text: The witnessed past: -di
Called görülen geçmiş (seen past), -di tells what you witnessed directly. Pattern: root + -di + person. Everything is glued on and harmonised.

Negation: <tur>gelmedim</tur> (I did not come), with the familiar -me. Watch the vowel harmonies: <tur>baktım</tur> (I looked), <tur>koştum</tur> (I ran), <tur>içtim</tur> (I drank), <tur>öptüm</tur>… (I kissed: the famous song).
The reported past: -miş
Here is a gem of Turkish: the duyulan geçmiş (heard past). It is used when you report an event you did not see yourself, or to express surprise.

items.fr: It rained, apparently. (I did not see it)
Ali is said to have got married! (I have just heard)
Apparently he was very tired.
Once upon a time… (the opening of folk tales)

blocks.text: French « paraît-il / aurait / se serait » ≈ -miş. In Turkish, saying « Ali geldi » (I saw him arrive) versus « Ali gelmiş » (I was told he had arrived) distinguishes the source of the information: a nuance French lacks, and one Turks consider essential!
Talking about your day

items.fr: I got up early in the morning.
I had breakfast, then I studied.
In the evening I met up with friends.
We had a lot of fun!

lines.name: Elif
lines.fr: What did you do at the weekend?

lines.name: Magloire
lines.tr: Cumartesi sinemaya gittim. Film çok güzeldi.
lines.fr: On Saturday I went to the cinema. The film was really good.

lines.name: Elif
lines.fr: Which film did you see?

lines.name: Magloire
lines.fr: The new Turkish comedy. I laughed a lot!

lines.name: Elif
lines.fr: I heard about it too, apparently it's very funny.

lines.name: Magloire
lines.tr: Evet! Pazar günü ise evde kaldım ve dinlendim.
lines.fr: Yes! On Sunday, though, I stayed at home and rested.

lines.name: Elif
lines.tr: Bence en doğru karar. Ben de yorgundum, hiçbir şey yapmadım.
lines.fr: In my opinion that was the best decision. I was tired too, I did nothing.

quiz.exp: git + -ti + -m: I went. (the root git- keeps its t → gitti, not « gitedi »)

opts: that I saw Ali get married
that I was told Ali got married
that Ali is going to get married
quiz.exp: -miş = reported past: I know it from an indirect source.
-me slips in before the ending: gel-me-dik.
It is the Turkish « once upon a time », in the reported past, as it should be for stories.
gül (to laugh) + -d + -üm: güldüm.

items.title: The future & projects
items.subtitle: -ecek, essential little words, and on towards B1

blocks.text: The future: -ecek / -acak

Look at geleceğim: the k of « gelecek » becomes ğ when a vowel follows. General rule: a final k softens to ğ before a vowel (yapacak → yapacağım). This is consonant alternation: Turkish loves to soften its final consonants.
Negation: <tur>gelmeyeceğim</tur> (I will not come): -me slips in, and the k turns back into… k! (gel-me-y-ecek-im). Question: <tur>Gelecek misin?</tur> (will you come?).
Talking about plans

items.fr: Tomorrow I will do some sport.
Next week I have an exam.
Next month I will go to Turkey.
Tonight I will stay at home.

blocks.text: The little words that change everything

You have finished the A1→B1 path! You can now introduce yourself, count, conjugate in the three main tenses, negate, ask questions, order at a restaurant and talk about your day. The logical next step: build your vocabulary with the flashcards, review the reference grammar, and above all: speak. Türkçe konuşmak istiyorsan, konuş! One Turk who corrects you is worth a thousand exercises. Bol şans! (Good luck!)
